subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Optimism Bias
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Optimism Bias.

hook.text: Newlyweds estimate their divorce chance at near zero. Actual divorce rate: close to 40%.

buildup.text: Weinstein found that people consistently underestimate their risk of negative events like illness or job loss.

discovery.text: Optimism bias: we believe bad things happen to other people, not to us. It feels like realism.

twist.text: Some optimism bias is healthy. It keeps us trying. But it also makes us skip insurance and seatbelts.

climax.text: The sweet spot: hopeful enough to act, realistic enough to prepare. Pure optimism is a gamble.

punchline.text: Hope isn't a plan. Prepare anyway.

quiz.question: What does optimism bias cause us to do?
options: Overestimate the likelihood of negative events
Underestimate our risk of negative events

details.summary: Optimism bias is the tendency to believe that negative events are less likely to happen to you than to others and that positive events are more likely. Most people expect better-than-average outcomes for themselves across health, career, and relationships.
details.whyItMatters: Optimism bias drives underinsurance, inadequate savings, risky business ventures, and insufficient safety precautions. People plan for best cases rather than realistic cases, leading to systematic under-preparation for negative outcomes.
takeaways: People consistently underestimate their personal risk for negative events
Optimism bias is one of the most robust and widespread cognitive biases
It drives underinsurance, under-saving, and excessive risk-taking

faq.question: Is optimism bias always harmful?
faq.answer: No. Moderate optimism increases persistence, resilience, and mental health. Entrepreneurs need optimism to attempt risky ventures that drive economic growth. The harm comes when optimism prevents realistic risk assessment and preparation.

faq.question: Can optimism bias be corrected?
faq.answer: Partially. Providing vivid, personalized risk information and asking people to imagine specific negative scenarios helps. But optimism bias is deeply functional for mental health, so complete correction is neither possible nor necessarily desirable.
